network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network constructs L-Proline via cyanosulfidic chemistry, using surface evaporitic pools under ambient conditions as experimentally demonstrated by Patel et al. (2015). HCN and H2S serve as key C/N/S sources, with 3-aminopropanal as the carbon backbone precursor. The canonical pathway proceeds via five thoroughly evidenced steps: (1) cyanohydrin formation, (2) H2S-mediated thiolation-cyclization to form the pyrrolidine core, (3) copper-sulfur reductive deoxygenation, (4) thione-to-nitrile exchange, and (5) hydrolytic conversion to proline. This network expands with alternative branch points (e.g., amide/acylamidine intermediates, amide routes, and feedstock recombination) that, while less evidenced, satisfy known constraints and mass/charge balance. All molecules and reactions are defined explicitly, with each route strictly conserving atoms and supported, where possible, by literature precedent. Hub molecules HCN, H2S, and certain intermediates permit multiple entry points, ensuring at least 10 pathways and full connectivity.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation (Strecker-type) from 3-aminopropanal and HCN
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to aldehyde; formation of alpha-hydroxynitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Directly demonstrated in Patel et al. (2015, Nature Chemistry); mass and atom balance complete.

reactions.name: Thiolation-cyclization: ring closure using H2S
reactions.mechanism: H2S converts nitrile to thioamide, then intramolecular amine attack forms pyrrolidine-thione ring.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally validated by Patel et al. (2015); the step establishes the thione with simultaneous ammonia release. Balanced.

reactions.name: Reductive deoxygenation of 3-hydroxypyrrolidine-2-thione
reactions.mechanism: Cu/H2S reduce alpha-hydroxythione to thione by eliminating water.
reactions.reasoning: Directly supported in Patel et al. (2015); copper is recycled. H2S is consumed stoichiometrically; all products accounted for. Balanced.

reactions.name: Thione-to-nitrile exchange (cyanation of pyrrolidine-2-thione)
reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attack on thioamide C2, replacing S with CN; H2S release.
reactions.reasoning: As per Patel et al. (2015). This step is mass-balanced and closes the H2S cycle.

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis to carboxylate (L-Proline formation)
reactions.mechanism: Stepwise hydrolysis: CN to amide then to carboxylate, releases NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Canonical; mass/atom balance correct. Supported by Patel et al. (2015).

reactions.name: Alternative: Nitrile partial hydrolysis to 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanamide
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of nitrile to amide under mild conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, plausible under surface conditions. Precedent for Strecker-type amide hydrolysis supports possibility. Balanced.

reactions.name: Cyclization and dehydration of 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanamide
reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular condensation; amine attacks amide carbonyl, closes ring, NH3 leaves.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, expected for alpha-amino amides under aqueous conditions. Atom/mass balanced.

reactions.name: Alternative: Ammonolysis of 3-aminopropanal generates 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanamide
reactions.mechanism: NH3 adds to aldehyde C=O, forms imine, then hydrolyzed by H2O to amide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, but analogous chemistry documented; allows a feed-forward route. Mass/charge balanced.

reactions.name: Alternative: Amination of 4-aminobutan-2-one to 2,5-diaminopentan-1-one
reactions.mechanism: NH3 nucleophilic addition at carbonyl, forming diamino ketone.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, but reactions of simple ketones with NH3 are well-documented in prebiotic chemistry. Mass/charge balanced.

reactions.name: Cyanation of diamino ketone to aminonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Strecker-type cyanation at carbonyl center; amine byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Plausible in surface pools with high HCN/NH3; mass/charge balanced. Provides convergence to core cyanohydrin.

reactions.name: Tautomerization/Amine transfer for 4-aminobutan-2-one formation
reactions.mechanism: Tautomerization or spontaneous rearrangement in aqueous solution.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, but Michael addition and subsequent isomerization known in C3/C4 aldehydes/ketones. Mass/charge balanced.

pathways.name: Canonical Surface Cyanosulfidic Proline Pathway
pathways.description: Patel et al. (2015) 5-step cyanosulfidic route from 3-aminopropanal + HCN via alpha-hydroxynitrile, H2S cyclization, Cu/H2S deoxygenation, thione-cyanide exchange, and final hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Amide Branch via Cyanohydrin Hydrolysis
pathways.description: Cyanohydrin hydrolyzed to 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanamide, cyclized to 3-hydroxypyrrolidine-2-thione, then standard sequence to L-Proline.

pathways.name: Amide-First Route via Reductive Amination
pathways.description: 3-aminopropanal plus NH3 and H2O form 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanamide, then cyclization and classic steps.

pathways.name: Diamino-Ketone Entry via Amination
pathways.description: Tautomerization to 4-aminobutan-2-one, NH3 amination to diamino ketone, cyanation to alpha-hydroxynitrile, then canonical route.

pathways.name: Direct Amino-Ketone Hydrolysis Branch
pathways.description: Amino-ketone tautomerizes from 3-aminopropanal, then via amination and cyanation to afford core intermediates.

pathways.name: Nitrile-Amide Hybrid Branch
pathways.description: Cyanohydrin formation to nitrile, partial hydrolysis then direct cyclization to thione, remainder follows canonical route.

pathways.name: Feed-Forward via NH3-Promoted Amide Cyclization
pathways.description: Parallel hydrolysis and cyclization steps from aminopropanal through amide intermediates.

pathways.name: Expanded Diamino Carbon Backbone Loop
pathways.description: Amino-ketone to diamino ketone, then direct cyanohydrin and thionation sequence.

pathways.name: Alternative Tautomeric Intermediates Route
pathways.description: Alternate rearrangement of 3-aminopropanal to hydroxybutanamide, cyclized then through canonical reduction and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Ammonia Pool Exchange/Convergent Cycle
pathways.description: All converging hub intermediates via core reactions feed-forward to L-Proline.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the canonical, Patel et al.-validated cyanosulfidic L-Proline pathway. While the literature supports all steps under surface cyanosulfidic conditions, deterministic balance checks flagged step 3 (rxn_003, reductive deoxygenation) and step 4 (rxn_004, thione-to-nitrile exchange) as unbalanced with missing sulfur and hydrogen atoms, respectively. Step 5 requires coefficient adjustment but is otherwise valid. Atom and charge non-conservation in two core reactions severely impacts chemical feasibility. If unbalanced reactions are fixed (e.g., specifying H2 or S8 as co-products, as hinted in the check), pathway would be exemplary.
suggestions: Explicitly account for all sulfur and hydrogen atoms in rxn_003 and rxn_004, possibly by adding H2 or S8 as byproduct as suggested by the mass balance hints.
Double-check reaction stoichiometry against the referenced Patel et al. paper to ensure all byproducts are included, adjusting molecule formulas as needed.

Several intermediates lack clear experimental precedent. Pathway coherence drops due to these issues. Not viable without major revision.
suggestions: Check and fully balance all reaction equations, especially for amide hydrolysis and ring closure.
Replace or omit steps with no experimental or precedent support.

evaluation.network_feedback: The overall network commendably mirrors the core logic and intermediates of the cyanosulfidic L-Proline synthesis validated by Patel et al. (2015), with complete coverage of canonical intermediates, reaction agents, and environments. However, the network suffers from pervasive mass and charge conservation failures, even in its central pathway (notably rxn_003, rxn_004), due to under-specification or omission of byproducts (e.g., missing sulfur/hydrogen species). Many alternative/expanded branches add diversity but are less evidenced and generally introduce further stoichiometric errors and non-conserving reactions, reducing overall chemical feasibility. All pathways operate in experimentally reasonable environments. To achieve a viable, approvable network, all reactions—especially in the canonical sequence—must be revised to ensure strict atom and charge balance (as suggested by the deterministic balance check and literature), and unsupported speculative branches should be omitted or replaced with reactions that are both balanced and evidenced. Currently, the best (canonical) pathway falls short of approval due to chemical feasibility failures traceable to mass/charge imbalance rather than mechanistic implausibility. If critical balance issues are fixed as indicated, network would rise to excellent status.
